definitions.label: Appeal to authority
definitions.definition: Relying on a person or institution's status as if it settles the argument, especially when the relevant evidence, expertise, or consensus has not been shown.

definitions.label: Argument from ignorance
definitions.definition: Treating a claim as true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved, rather than supplying positive evidence.

definitions.label: Begging the question
definitions.definition: Assuming, directly or indirectly, the very point that needs to be established, so the conclusion is smuggled into the premises.

definitions.label: Equivocation
definitions.definition: Shifting the meaning of a key word or phrase during the argument, making the reasoning seem stronger than it is.

definitions.label: Red herring
definitions.definition: Diverting attention from the issue under dispute to a related but less relevant point, leaving the original challenge insufficiently answered.

definitions.label: Special pleading
definitions.definition: Applying an exception or different standard to one side of the argument without giving a principled reason for the difference.

definitions.label: Ambiguity effect
definitions.definition: Preferring clearer or more familiar claims over uncertain ones, even when the uncertain option may deserve serious consideration.

definitions.label: Authority bias
definitions.definition: Giving extra weight to a claim because it comes from a perceived authority, sometimes beyond what the evidence itself supports.

definitions.label: Base-rate neglect
definitions.definition: Underweighting general background rates or prior probabilities while focusing too heavily on a vivid specific case or local detail.

definitions.label: Belief bias
definitions.definition: Judging an argument by whether its conclusion feels believable instead of evaluating whether the conclusion follows from the premises.

definitions.label: Confirmation bias
definitions.definition: Seeking, interpreting, or remembering evidence in ways that favor an existing view while discounting contrary information.

definitions.label: Scope neglect
definitions.definition: Failing to adjust judgment in proportion to the scale, number, or magnitude of what is being discussed.

definitions.label: Subjective validation
definitions.definition: Treating a claim as especially accurate or meaningful because it feels personally resonant or confirms one's private experience.

moves.speaker: Stuart Knechtle
moves.proposition: God supplies enough intellectual and affective evidence for a free response, while overwhelming manifestation would yield mere assent rather than trusting relationship.

sourceSpan.excerpt: talks about how God gives us just enough evidence to connect with our heads and our hearts in order for us to make a free decision rather than coercively just showing up and saying you better believe in me here it is no I'm right here right now and secondly but Matt's secondly to that point that's simply going to be a type of mental Ascent that you're going to buy into there's not going to be any type of trusting relationship simply by him proving himself to you right now by showing up right next to your chair just like in Matthew 28 so many of his disciples actually connected with him physically after he rose from the dead and yet they stopped believing just a matter of probably Weeks Later

responseComponents.text: God's not supplying coercively conclusive manifestation is presented as compatible with supplying enough evidence for free, relational trust.

moves.argumentDescription: Knechtle argues that God provides sufficient intellectual and affective evidence for freely chosen trust, whereas undeniable manifestation would secure only assent, not relationship.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle directly confronts Dillahunty’s communicative-God challenge by distinguishing propositional assent from voluntarily relational trust, while Matthew 28 suggests physical encounter need not produce enduring belief. Principal limitation: Neither the claim that resurrection witnesses soon abandoned belief nor “just enough evidence” establishes an assessable threshold; moreover, clearer disclosure is characterized as coercive without addressing intermediate possibilities or nonresistant uncertainty. Live burden: Knechtle must demonstrate that Christianity’s intellectual and affective indicators are sufficient, explain why stronger yet resistible evidence would damage freely chosen relationship, and connect his disciples comparison to divine hiddenness. Locked score: 70 rewards direct engagement and substantial motion-level relevance, while weak evidential grounding, undefined calibration, and incomplete contact with Dillahunty’s objection keep this coherent distinction from establishing Christianity’s rationality.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Internal consistency alone cannot confer relevant rationality; a belief must also be consistent with the facts of reality.

sourceSpan.excerpt: but internal consistency isn't enough um Fantasy games with a rule setting for their magic system can be internally consistent Mario is internally consistent you have a certain jump height maximum run down maximum even using the game uh glitches to to do a speed run is consistent which is why you can have tool assisted speed runs sorry if I'm getting all geeky on everybody but it would be irrational to claim that Mario can violate the rules of the game or if you prefer Dungeons and Dragons has a magic system and a set of rules that govern that aspect of the game and as long as an act within the game is consistent with those rules it's rational that type of rationality does us no good internal consistency isn't relevant to what we're talking about today in order for something to be rational it needs to be consistent with the facts of reality

moves.argumentDescription: By comparing coherent fictional rule systems with actual belief, Dillahunty argues that rationality demands more than internal consistency: claims must fit reality’s facts.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s Mario and Dungeons and Dragons comparisons sharply expose the inferential gap between coherence under invented rules and rational warrant about an external world, fixing the motion’s epistemic standard. Principal limitation: Those examples demonstrate that internal consistency is insufficient, but they neither specify which factual correspondence counts nor establish that Christianity fails it, while “irrelevant” understates coherence’s screening role. Live burden: He must supply a defensible test distinguishing mere compatibility with reality from evidential confirmation, then apply that test to Christianity rather than leaving the external comparison implicit. Locked score: 84 appropriately reflects exceptional burden relevance and responsiveness, strong clarity and coherence, but only moderate evidential support and slightly compressed calibration in the positive reality-based standard.

moves.speaker: Stuart Knechtle
moves.proposition: Knechtle's return to Christianity followed what he describes as a multifaceted evidential reassessment and rejection of hedonism's inadequacy.

sourceSpan.excerpt: and so for me coming back to the faith and ultimately deciding against hedonism and the bankruptcy behind it was what I've given you in terms of all of a sudden I saw all this evidence

responseComponents.text: Knechtle presents his return as a response to an accumulated body of evidence rather than internal consistency alone.
His reported reconsideration asserts that evidence was available and sufficient for him after critical distance from his upbringing.

moves.argumentDescription: Knechtle presents his return to Christianity as the result of accumulated evidence and rejecting hedonism as bankrupt, thereby asserting that faith had rational warrant.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle’s first-person sequence—rejecting hedonism’s “bankruptcy,” then returning after seeing “all this evidence”—intelligibly challenges Dillahunty’s claim that Christianity lacks warrant. Principal limitation: Neither the evidence nor hedonism’s alleged inadequacy is specified, and abandoning hedonism does not establish Christianity; consequently, it never meets Dillahunty’s reality-consistency test or demand for verifiable support. Live burden: Knechtle must identify the considerations, explain how they connect rejection of hedonism to Christian belief, and demonstrate why they remain assessable beyond the private force of his conversion experience. Locked score: 64 recognizes clear autobiographical structure, measured personal framing, reply contact, and motion relevance, while reserving substantial credit because the decisive evidence is unauditable here, the comparative inference is incomplete, and the opponent’s evidential standard remains unanswered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A return to faith after seeing evidence is internally intelligible, but rejecting hedonism and finding Christianity warranted are joined without an explicit inferential bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The autobiographical report supplies first-person evidence of reconsideration, yet 'all this evidence' is unspecified within this move and cannot be independently assessed.

responsiveness.rationale: It contests the claim that no warrant was available by reporting personal evidential reassessment, but does not answer the opponent's public reality-testing standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The account is relevant to whether Knechtle personally found Christianity warranted, but autobiographical conviction alone only partially advances the general motion.

precisionClarity.rationale: The personal sequence of leaving hedonism and returning to faith is clear, while the decisive evidence and the meaning of hedonism's bankruptcy remain vague.

calibrationCharity.rationale: The speaker appropriately frames the claim as his own experience, but the compressed characterization of hedonism as bankrupt is asserted rather than fairly developed.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Because Christianity posits a communicative agent able to supply a rational model but no such evidential explanation has appeared, its burden of proof remains unmet.

moves.argumentDescription: Dillahunty argues that Christianity’s allegedly communicative God has not delivered verifiable support or a justifying explanation, so Christianity has not discharged its rational burden.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty turns God’s claimed communicative capacity into an evidential expectation and connects its alleged nonfulfillment directly to rational withholding, yielding unusually strong responsiveness and motion-level burden relevance. Principal limitation: Although the excerpt says Christian claims lack “evidence or verifiable observation,” it neither examines the proffered evidence nor defends why divine communication should produce Dillahunty’s particular public, falsifiable model. Live burden: He must specify what adequate disclosure would involve, justify the expectation from God’s capacities, and demonstrate that disputed experiences and arguments genuinely fail that standard. Locked score: A 78 appropriately rewards the intelligible inference and exceptionally direct debate contact while withholding credit because the pivotal absence claim is asserted broadly, with limited precision and charitable engagement.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Whether a belief is rational can differ between people because evidentiary warrant depends on the evidence available to each person, even if the underlying proposition has one objective truth value.

sourceSpan.excerpt: of whether or not he is warranted and is rational in believing it our foundation of what is rational is based on what evidence we actually have so it is possible for a God to exist and choose to reveal himself to Steward in a way that Stewart can have evidential warrant and not reveal himself to me uh so that I don't have evidential warrant but if I were to believe in that circumstance I would be behaving irrational irrationally my belief would be irrational

moves.argumentDescription: Dillahunty argues that rational belief tracks each person’s available evidence, so the same objectively true proposition may warrant belief for one person but not another.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty sharply separates objective truth from person-relative rational warrant: God could exist, reveal himself convincingly to Knechtle, withhold comparable evidence from Dillahunty, and thereby rationally differentiate their beliefs. Principal limitation: This hypothetical demonstrates conceptual possibility, not either participant’s actual evidence, while leaving the evidential threshold distinguishing justified acceptance from irrational belief materially underdeveloped. Live burden: Dillahunty must identify which publicly assessable or privately accessible considerations justify withholding his belief, explain how conflicting revelations should be evaluated, and connect that account to his central reality test. Locked score: The 86 properly rewards exceptional calibration, inferential coherence, precise exposition, and relevant clarification while preserving an evidentiary discount because the example maps possible unequal access more convincingly than it establishes anyone’s actual warrant.

responseComponents.text: A report that Jesus forgave sins cannot establish either his unity with the Father or an actual forgiveness event.

moves.argumentDescription: Dillahunty argues that a preserved Gospel report alone establishes neither Jesus’s unity with the Father nor the occurrence and efficacy of supernatural forgiveness.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty isolates the equivocation between transmission of a report and establishment of its supernatural content, answering Knechtle’s manuscript defense and appeal to Jesus forgiving sins. Live burden: He must articulate criteria for moving from testimony to theological actuality, then show why manuscript abundance, early dating, and patristic quotation cannot meet them without treating testimony as worthless. Locked score: The 86 reflects exceptional responsiveness and strong coherence, relevance, clarity, and charity, while weaker evidential warrant preserves the unresolved challenge of specifying confirmatory evidence for forgiveness itself.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Historical evidence need not be empirically verifiable, and its strength can increase with multiple sources, especially when competing parties independently report consistent facts.

sourceSpan.excerpt: what is my definition of historical evidence I think I probably need the context in which to use but basically it is uh evidence from the past that is the best that we have currently well I mean I guess suppose it wouldn't necessarily be the best so historical evidence is evidence that isn't necessarily empirically verifiable but is reported from the past and we can uh for historical claims we can look at um for example who's making the claim how many different sources is it coming from is it coming from competing sources and the stronger the uh the evidence is stronger when you have for example the losing side saying here's what happened and The Winning Side saying here's what happened and those are consistent um because we don't have a time machine

moves.argumentDescription: Dillahunty treats past reports as gradable evidence, arguing that agreement among numerous genuinely competing sources increases confidence when direct empirical verification is unavailable.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s answer makes his testimony standard comparative rather than dismissive, expressly admitting reports from the empirically inaccessible past while explaining why concordance between numerous competing parties increases confidence. Principal limitation: The example never establishes that Gospel accounts are independent, adversarial, or insulated from common traditions, and his self-correction leaves provenance, genre, and reporter reliability insufficiently specified. Live burden: To reinforce his testimony objection, Dillahunty must apply these criteria to debated sources, distinguish numerical plurality from evidential independence, and demonstrate whether cross-party consistency materially improves Christianity’s warrant. Locked score: 82 appropriately rewards the coherent qualification, direct answer, source comparison, and charitable calibration, while comparatively weaker precision and evidential support reflect missing Gospel-level application and unresolved dependence questions.
